props.title: Car Paradox
lines: You want the car because of how you think it makes others see you.
They are looking at the car, not at you.

props.title: What a $100,000 car actually signals
items: Someone driving a $100,000 car might be wealthy — or might have $100,000 less, or $100,000 more debt.
Humble: you want respect. The paradox: observers respect the car, not the driver.
Rich is a current income. Wealth is unspent options. They look the same from the curb until they do not.
If the point was admiration, the book says: skip the car and keep the assets that actually buy freedom.

props.title: What you think you bought vs what they saw

left.name: What you wanted
lines: Respect, status, proof you made it.
A $100,000 car as a loud résumé.

right.name: What they saw
lines: The car. Not your skill, not your savings rate, not your name.
They may want the same car next. You were the billboard, not the hero.
If admiration was the goal, unspent wealth buys more of it over decades than chrome does in a minute.

props.title: Keep the respect trade honest
items: Spending to be liked is a tax. The audience is looking at the object.
Rich and wealthy look identical at a stoplight. Only the unspent pile is wealth.
If the car requires debt that can force a sale, you bought the opposite of freedom.

rows.v: People buy loud goods hoping the object will transfer respect onto the owner.
Observers usually stop at the object. They imagine themselves in the seat, not you.
If the object is financed, you may have purchased the opposite of the freedom you wanted to display.
Unspent wealth does not photograph. That is why it is easy to under-count and over-spend.
If admiration was the goal, keep the assets that buy time. Chrome is a billboard for the factory.
